subject: Climate & Environment
title: Perovskite: The Next Solar Revolution
description: A micro-lesson that makes Perovskite: The Next Solar Revolution usable.

hook.text: Silicon panels are great. But a crystal discovered in 1839 could make them obsolete.

buildup.text: Perovskite solar cells can be printed like ink on flexible sheets at low temperatures.

discovery.text: In just 15 years of research, perovskite efficiency jumped from 3.8% to over 33%.

twist.text: The catch: perovskites degrade quickly in moisture and heat. Durability is the bottleneck.

climax.text: Stacking perovskite on silicon creates tandem cells that break efficiency records.

punchline.text: The future of solar might be printed like a newspaper.

quiz.question: What is the main challenge for perovskite solar cells?
options: They degrade in moisture and heat
They only work in cold climates

details.summary: Perovskite solar cells use a crystal structure that can be printed onto flexible surfaces at low cost and high speed. They have reached lab efficiencies above 26 percent in just over a decade of development and could be layered on top of silicon cells to push combined efficiency past 30 percent.
details.whyItMatters: Perovskites could make solar panels cheaper, lighter, and more versatile. Tandem perovskite-silicon cells may define the next generation of solar technology.
takeaways: Perovskite cells can be manufactured at very low cost
Lab efficiency has risen from 3 to over 26 percent in a decade
Tandem cells combining perovskite and silicon exceed 30 percent

faq.question: What is stopping perovskite panels from reaching the market?
faq.answer: Stability is the main challenge. Perovskites degrade when exposed to moisture, heat, and UV light. Encapsulation and compositional tweaks are improving durability. Lead content also raises environmental concerns that researchers are working to address.

faq.question: How do tandem solar cells work?
faq.answer: A perovskite layer on top captures high-energy blue and green photons, while the silicon layer below captures lower-energy red and infrared light. Together they use more of the solar spectrum, boosting efficiency beyond what either material achieves alone.
